query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor concentration (≈0.1 at.%) of boron to equal-atomic NbMoTaW will improve its room-temperature ductility by promoting the formation of fine boride precipitates at grain boundaries that enhance their cohesion, without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW exhibiting a single-phase BCC structure with excellent high-temperature (1600 °C) strength and irradiation resistance (as predicted by first-principles) but very poor room-temperature ductility.
generation.intervention: Introduce ≈0.1 atomic percent boron during alloy synthesis.
generation.conditions: Evaluations under room-temperature conditions, high-temperature (1600 °C) mechanical tests, and simulated irradiation conditions (e.g., ion irradiation) to mimic neutron-induced damage.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of finely dispersed boride precipitates (analogous to (Hf, Zr)B2 observed in similar refractory high-entropy alloys) selectively at grain boundaries, while retaining the BCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: Boron segregates to the grain boundaries and reacts with alloying elements to form stable, fine boride phases. These precipitates enhance grain-boundary cohesion and inhibit intergranular cracking, thus improving ductility at room temperature. The low concentration of boron minimizes any adverse modifications in the BCC matrix, thereby preserving high-temperature strength and irradiation resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated NbMoTaW, the boron-modified alloy will exhibit significantly improved room-temperature ductility, maintain or slightly enhance its high-temperature mechanical performance at 1600 °C, and show no reduction in irradiation resistance.
generation.baseline: Untreated, equal-atomic NbMoTaW alloy with significant room-temperature brittleness but strong high-temperature performance and predicted irradiation resilience.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective only at low boron concentrations (~0.1 at.%). Excessive boron may lead to the formation of coarse or excessive brittle borides, potentially degrading both room-temperature ductility and high-temperature strength. The hypothesis applies to alloys with similar elemental distributions and processing histories.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the exact identity and stability of the boride precipitates that form in NbMoTaW, as well as the long-term effects of boron under cyclic thermal loading and irradiation. The interactions between irradiation-induced defects and the new boride phases also require further clarification.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of equal-atomic NbMoTaW alloys under identical conditions: one set with ≈0.1 at.% boron and the other without boron. Thoroughly characterize microstructures (via TEM, XRD) to identify boride precipitates at the grain boundaries. Conduct mechanical testing at room temperature and 1600 °C, and perform ion irradiation experiments to simulate neutron damage.
measurements: Microstructural characterization (XRD, TEM, SEM) to detect and analyze grain-boundary precipitates
Room-temperature tensile tests to measure ductility and work hardening behavior
High-temperature (1600 °C) mechanical tests (e.g., compression or tensile) to assess strength retention
Post-irradiation examination (e.g., hardness, microstructural stability, and defect density analysis) to evaluate irradiation resistance
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if: (a) the boron-added alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility compared to the baseline; (b) there is a measurable degradation in high-temperature mechanical performance; or (c) the irradiation resistance is compromised relative to the untreated NbMoTaW alloy.

cited_evidence.text:
## Abstract
AbstractTo develop strong refractory high-entropy alloys for use at elevated temperatures as well as to overcome grain-boundary brittleness, an equimolar HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was prepared, and a minor amount of boron (0.1 at.%) was added into the alloy. The microstructures of the alloys were characterized, and their macro-to-microscale mechanical properties were measured. The microstructural observations indicated that the matrices of both the alloys were composed of a body-centered cubic solid-solution structure, and the added boron induced the precipitation of hexagonal close-packed borides (most likely the (Hf, Zr)B2) at the grain boundaries. The modulus and hardness of differently oriented grains were about equivalent, suggesting a diminished anisotropy, and many small slips occurred on multiple {110} planes. While the hardness of the matrix was not increased, the intergranular precipitation of the borides markedly raised the hardness of the grain boundaries. Owing to the enhanced grain boundary cohesion, the work hardenability and ductility were effectively improved with the addition of boron.Keywords: refractory alloy, high-entropy alloy, boride, grain boundary, mec
